## Remote Interviewing

Remote interviews are no longer a pandemic workaround. For much knowledge-work hiring they are routine, and the quality of your video process shapes how candidates see you. This article quotes no adoption figures, because we have not cited a source for any.

### Technical Setup

For interviewers:

- A good webcam
- An external microphone or quality headset
- Good lighting
- A professional, clean background
- Stable internet, tested before each interview
- A backup plan, such as a phone number or alternative platform

Platform selection:

- Zoom: widely used, with recording capability
- Google Meet: integrated with calendar
- Microsoft Teams: common in enterprises
- Specialized tools such as CoderPad or HackerRank for technical interviews

This list is examples only, not an endorsement.

### Creating an Excellent Remote Experience

#### Before the Interview

- Send the calendar invite with the video link at least a day in advance
- Include the interviewer's name, title and professional profile
- Share the interview agenda and what to prepare
- Provide technical requirements such as browser and software
- Send a "what to expect" guide for candidates unfamiliar with your process

#### During the Interview

- Start on time, since even a couple of minutes late feels unprofessional remotely
- Turn your camera on and model the behavior you expect
- Begin with small talk to build rapport, which is harder to achieve remotely
- Share your screen when discussing anything visual
- Check in periodically ("Can you hear me okay?")
- Allow for natural pauses, since latency makes people talk over each other

#### After the Interview

- Thank the candidate promptly
- Provide a clear timeline for next steps
- Send feedback within the committed timeframe
- Follow up even if the timeline slips

### Remote-Specific Assessment Adjustments

| Traditional signal | Remote equivalent |
|---|---|
| Firm handshake | Warm greeting, eye contact with the camera |
| Body language reading | Facial expressions, tone of voice |
| Whiteboard problem-solving | Virtual whiteboard |
| Office tour and culture | Video tour, team virtual coffee |
| In-person presentation | Screen-share presentation |
| Portfolio review | Screen-share walkthrough |

### Managing Bias in Remote Interviews

Remote interviews introduce new biases:

- **Technology bias:** judging candidates by their home setup or internet quality
- **Background bias:** making assumptions based on what is visible behind them
- **Audio quality bias:** penalizing candidates with imperfect audio
- **Camera comfort bias:** favoring candidates who are comfortable on video

Mitigate by:

- Standardizing evaluation criteria and focusing on content, not delivery medium
- Giving candidates guidance on technical setup
- Offering flexibility, such as camera-optional for initial screens
- Training interviewers on remote-specific biases

### Panel Interviews Over Video

Remote panel interviews need special consideration:

- Keep the number of interviewers on video small, since a large panel can feel intimidating
- Designate a moderator to manage turn-taking
- Use the chat for follow-up questions to reduce interruption
- Keep panels short to limit video fatigue
- Allow breaks between back-to-back sessions

### Recording and Compliance

- Always get consent before recording
- State your recording policy in the interview invitation
- Follow local laws, since consent rules vary by jurisdiction
- Store recordings securely with limited access
- Define a retention period and follow it
